intro/hello: Every network so far has had a fixed shape.
intro/fixed: One image in, one set of class scores out.
intro/world: But much of the world arrives as a sequence: the words of a sentence, the frames of a video, the characters of a program.
intro/length: A sentence can be four words long, or forty. To read one, a network needs memory.
intro/trick: A recurrent network reads one element at a time, and folds each into a running summary: its hidden state.
intro/hidden: Hidden, because nothing outside sees or supervises it directly: the network learns what to keep there.
intro/same: The same weights do the folding at every step, so it can read a sequence of any length, and we read answers off the memory.
intro/karpathy: This chapter follows Andrej Karpathy's 2016 lecture, and the tiny script that made these models famous.
intro/plan: We will teach a model to write fake Shakespeare, see why it forgets, meet the L S T M that fixes it, and have a network describe photos in words.
shapes/cols: Draw each time step as a column: input x at the bottom, hidden state h in the middle, output y on top.
shapes/arrows: Arrows between the hidden states carry memory forward, and every column shares the same weights.
shapes/one: One to one is no sequence at all: the image classifiers so far.
shapes/cap: One to many is image captioning: one image in, then a word per step, each fed back in as the next input.
shapes/sent: Many to one reads a review word by word, then judges its mood: sentiment classification.
shapes/mt: Many to many reads a whole English sentence, then writes it in French, with its own length and word order: translation.
shapes/vid: And in step, one output per input: labeling each frame of a video, with memory of the frames before it.
shapes/glimpse: Even a fixed size input can be read in pieces. One model reads house numbers by steering a small glimpse around the image. Another paints digits, stroke by stroke.
recurrence/rule: At the heart of every recurrent network is one update rule, applied at every time step.
recurrence/read: Take the old memory, h from the step before, and the new input, x.
recurrence/f: Feed both to a function f with weights W, and out comes the new memory.
recurrence/same: And it is the same function, with the same weights, at every step.
recurrence/acc: If you program, you know this shape: a loop with a running total, folding in one more input per pass.
recurrence/learn: Only here, f is a small layer with learned weights, so the network learns what is worth remembering.
recurrence/unroll: To see it as an ordinary network, unroll the loop: one copy of f per step, wired head to tail.
recurrence/deep: That is a deep network with one layer per step, and one twist: every layer shares the same weights.
recurrence/grad: So in training, the weights collect a gradient from every copy, and those gradients simply add up.
vanilla/simple: The simplest f is one fully connected layer and a tan h: the vanilla R N N.
vanilla/whh: The matrix W h h mixes the old memory: each new number is a weighted sum of all the old ones.
vanilla/wxh: W x h mixes in the new input, with weights of its own, and a bias is added.
vanilla/squash: Then tan h squashes every entry to between minus one and one, so the memory stays bounded.
vanilla/why: A third matrix, W h y, reads output scores off the new memory. Three matrices, and nothing else.
vanilla/curve: Tan h is an S shaped curve: steep in the middle, flat far away.
vanilla/slope: Its slope, one minus tan h squared, is one at the center and nearly zero in the flat parts. Remember those flat parts.
vanilla/shared: And remember W h h. Shared by every step, it lets one small network read text of any length, and it is what makes training hard.
hello/model: Now a concrete example: a model of text, which predicts the next character from the ones so far.
hello/tiny: Shrink the world to four letters, h, e, l and o, and one training word: hello.
hello/onehot: Each letter goes in as a one hot vector: all zeros, except a one in its own slot.
hello/targets: The targets are the input shifted by one: after h comes e, then l, then l, then o.
hello/trap: Look at the last two. The input is l both times, but the answers differ. Only memory can tell the first l from the second.
hello/step: So run it. At each step, the input and the memory mix through tan h into three hidden numbers.
hello/scores: W h y reads four scores off the memory, one per letter, and a softmax turns them into probabilities.
hello/loss: The loss at each step is minus the log of the probability given to the true next letter: zero if certain, large if surprised.
hello/sum: Summed over the word, blind guessing would cost about five and a half. These random weights do a little worse: five point eight two.
hello/trained: After three hundred small training steps, the loss falls to zero point zero six. Same input l, two different answers: the memory works.
sampling/gen: Once trained, the model can write. Give it a few characters to start from.
sampling/probs: It scores every possible next character, and the softmax turns scores into probabilities.
sampling/draw: Draw one at random, according to those probabilities. That is sampling.
sampling/feed: Then feed it back in as the next input, so everything it writes becomes context.
sampling/repeat: Repeat as long as you like. Here, a model trained on a few pages of Shakespeare writes on its own.
sampling/why: Always taking the top character instead gives the same text every time, and tends to get stuck repeating itself.
sampling/temp: A dial called temperature sets how bold the draws are: divide every score by T before the softmax.
sampling/low: Below one, the favorite grows even more likely: safe, repetitive text.
sampling/high: Above one, the odds even out: adventurous text, then nonsense.
sampling/same: The model never changes. Only how boldly we read it.
bptt/graph: Training an R N N is ordinary backprop on the unrolled graph. Here it has a grand name: backpropagation through time.
bptt/fwd: Run forward through the sequence, adding up the losses.
bptt/bwd: Then run backward, from the last step to the first.
bptt/two: A hidden state's gradient says how much the loss would move if we nudged it. This one reached the loss two ways: through its own output, and through the next hidden state.
bptt/own: So its gradient has two parts. One is the score gradient, probabilities minus the one hot target, pushed back through W h y.
bptt/next: The other arrives from the future as d h next, through tan h's slope and W h h, transposed.
bptt/acc: Each weight was used at every step, so its gradients from all the steps add up.
bptt/remember: Remember this: every step back multiplies the gradient by the same matrix.
bptt/truncate: A whole book per update would be slow. So we truncate: forward and backward through one chunk of twenty five characters at a time.
bptt/carry: The hidden state carries on into the next chunk, so the model still reads continuous text. The gradient stops at the chunk boundary.
bptt/price: The price: no direct learning signal about anything longer than a chunk.
minchar/gist: Karpathy wrote this whole model as one num pie file of about a hundred and twelve lines, with no framework.
minchar/parts: The vocabulary is the distinct characters of a text file, and the model is three small random matrices.
minchar/loop: It loops: take the next twenty five characters, run the loss forward and backward, and update.
minchar/clip: Gradients are clipped to plus or minus five, and the update is ada grad: each weight's step is divided by the root of its own running sum of squared gradients.
minchar/run: Here it learns from the opening of Shakespeare's Coriolanus, three thousand characters, printing samples as it goes.
minchar/i0: At first: random characters, and a loss right where blind guessing would put it.
minchar/i100: Within a hundred steps it knows which characters are common: lowercase letters and spaces.
minchar/i1000: By a thousand, short real words appear, like and, we and the, and lines begin to break.
minchar/i3000: By three thousand the loss has nearly halved, and a half spelled citizen ends in a colon and a new line, like a speaker in a play.
minchar/long: Ten times longer, it writes in the shape of a play. With only three pages to learn from, though, it soon starts reciting them.
learns/scale: Scale this up to a few layers of L S T Ms, hundreds of units each, and the results get eerie.
learns/shakes: On all of Shakespeare, it writes speaker names and archaic speeches: Shakespeare from across the room, nonsense up close.
learns/wiki: On Wikipedia: headings, links and invented citations. On the lay tech source of a geometry book: proofs that nearly compile.
learns/linux: On the Linux kernel: C code with balanced braces and comments. It was only ever given characters.
learns/watch: Why does it work? Karpathy, Johnson and Fei-Fei watched single memory cells as a network read, coloring each character by a cell's value.
learns/quote: Most cells were a jumble. But one switched on at an opening quote, and stayed on until the closing one.
learns/more: Another counted along each line. In C code, cells tracked if statements, comments, and how deeply the code was nested.
learns/ours: Nobody asked for these trackers: they helped predict the next character, so gradient descent built them. Our tiny model shows a faint version: its best unit loosely follows spaces.
captioning/halves: Now join the two halves of the course. A conv net turns an image into a vector, and an R N N turns a vector into a sentence.
captioning/cnn: In 2015, several groups did exactly that. Run the image through a conv net trained on ImageNet, and cut off its last layer.
captioning/v: Instead of a thousand class scores, keep the four thousand and ninety six numbers before them: the vector v.
captioning/cond: v enters the recurrence as one extra term, with its own weight matrix. Assignment 3 uses it to set the first hidden state instead.
captioning/start: Feed in a start token. Words go in as learned vectors, and the output scores every word in the vocabulary.
captioning/sample: Sample a word, feed it back, and stop when the network says end. In this toy, a small table plays the trained network.
captioning/coco: Train it end to end on Microsoft Coco: about a hundred and twenty thousand images, each captioned by five people.
captioning/good: Results are often startlingly good: a surfer riding a wave. But a captioner may add a frisbee that is not there, because frisbees go with parks.
captioning/glance: It knows captions better than images, and it glances at the image only once. Next chapter, attention lets it look again for every word.
vanishing/principle: In principle, a vanilla R N N can remember across hundreds of steps. In practice, it struggles beyond a dozen or so.
vanishing/loop: The reason is in the backward loop: to go k steps back, the gradient is multiplied by tan h's slope and by W h h transposed, k times over.
vanishing/numbers: Plain numbers first. One point one to the fiftieth power is a hundred and seventeen. Zero point nine to the fiftieth is five thousandths.
vanishing/sigma: A matrix does the same along its strongest direction. The stretch there is its largest singular value, sigma.
vanishing/explode: Above one, the gradient can grow exponentially as it travels back: exploding gradients, and absurdly large updates.
vanishing/vanish: Below one, it shrinks exponentially, and tan h's slopes only shrink it more: vanishing gradients. The early steps learn almost nothing.
vanishing/clip: For exploding gradients, clip: if the gradient's size passes a threshold, scale it down, keeping its direction. Our script clips each entry to five.
vanishing/arch: Vanishing needs a new architecture: a path back through time with no matrix multiply at every step.
lstm/two: The L S T M, from 1997, keeps two memories: the hidden state h that it shows the world, and a private cell state c.
lstm/gates: Gates control the cell: numbers between zero and one, computed fresh at every step, that act as soft switches.
lstm/one: One matrix multiply on the old hidden state and the new input gives four pieces. Three pass through a sigmoid: the input, forget and output gates.
lstm/g: The fourth, g, passes through tan h: the candidate values to write.
lstm/update: The update: multiply the old cell by the forget gate, to erase, then add the input gate times g, to write.
lstm/reveal: The hidden state is a squashed view of the cell, filtered by the output gate.
lstm/store: In this one unit L S T M with hand set weights, a store flag opens the input gate and shuts the forget gate, writing a new value.
lstm/hold: Otherwise the cell holds its value, losing under one percent a step. A trained L S T M learns weights like these by itself.
lstm/highway: Now go backward along the cell. The new cell is the forget gate times the old one, plus a term, so the gradient is just multiplied by the forget gate.
lstm/nomat: No matrix and no tan h slope, and the network can hold that gate near one for as long as it must. Like res net's skip connections, it is an additive highway.
lstm/gru: Its cousin, the G R U, merges cell and hidden state and uses two gates. Searches over thousands of variants found nothing clearly better.
outro/loop: To recap: a recurrent network is a loop, with a hidden state and the same weights at every step.
outro/gen: Trained to predict what comes next, it writes: sample, feed back, repeat.
outro/bptt: It trains with backprop through time, in chunks, with the memory carried forward.
outro/forget: Multiplying by W h h at every step makes plain R N Ns explode or forget: clipping fixes the first, the L S T M's additive cell the second.
outro/cap: And a conv net feeding an R N N writes captions, which you will build in Assignment 3.
outro/next: Next, attention. Instead of one glance at the image, the network chooses where to look, and looks again for every word it writes.
